title: Equation
summary: Equation is a cluster name for espionage activity described in public reporting as unusually well resourced, with tradecraft that treated malware as an engineering discipline rather than a disposable tool. Reporting documented modular implants, strong cryptography, multiple redundant persistence points, and, most consequentially, implant code that lived in device firmware rather than on the operating system. That placement matters operationally: firmware-resident code can survive disk formatting, operating system reinstallation, and many standard incident response procedures, and some published guidance concluded that affected hardware had to be replaced rather than cleaned. The activity was reported against telecommunications, aerospace, energy, military, and research targets across many countries. Detection is difficult because the artefacts sit below the operating system and standard endpoint agents may not have visibility there. The common misunderstanding is that wiping and reimaging a machine restores trust. If the implant is in firmware, reimaging removes evidence and may leave the intruder in place.

beginner.definition: Equation is a research name for an extremely well-funded cyber spying group. Public reports say it hid its code inside hardware firmware. Firmware is the small program that starts a device before the operating system loads.
beginner.whyItMatters: Hidden code in firmware survives wiping the disk and reinstalling the system. That means normal cleanup steps may not remove the attacker. Standard security tools often cannot see firmware at all. This makes recovery planning much harder and slower. It also means you must think about supply chain trust, not only about your own machines.
howItWorks: The attackers gain access to a target and study the hardware in use.
They install a hidden program that sits below the operating system, where few tools look.
That program can restart itself even after a full system reinstall and disk wipe.
It hides its network traffic inside ordinary communications, so it looks normal.
Modules are added later for listening, stealing files, and keeping long-term control.
Cleanup then usually means replacing the hardware, not only reinstalling the software.
beginner.example: Imagine a safe built into the wall of an office rather than standing on the floor. The safe stays where it is, untouched, still holding whatever was put inside. You can clean the room as often as you like and the contents remain. Firmware implants follow this logic. The operating system is the room that gets repainted, and the implant is the fixture behind the plaster. Rebuilding the room does not remove it, and you may never see it unless you inspect the structure itself.
takeaways: Wiping a disk does not always remove an attacker.
Some implants live below the operating system, where few tools look.
Recovery planning must consider hardware replacement in the worst case.

objectives: Explain what firmware is and why code placed there resists standard remediation.
Describe why disk reimaging may remove evidence without removing an implant.
Identify the visibility gaps that limit standard endpoint security tooling.
Explain how modular implant design supports many missions from one deployment.
Summarise how public reporting characterises the resources behind this activity.
Describe recovery decisions when persistent code may exist below the operating system.
